name: Robert Paul
milestone_by_age_26: Won the first of four consecutive World Championship gold medals in pairs figure skating with partner Barbara Wagner in 1957, at age 19.
early_history_summary: Paul began skating as a young child in Toronto after recovering from polio, when his parents bought him skates. He joined the Toronto Skating Club and was paired with Barbara Wagner at age 15 by coach Sheldon Galbraith, who trained them intensively with film analysis and mirror work. They won five consecutive Canadian national titles (1955-1960) and four World titles (1957-1960), plus Olympic gold in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in Toronto to a supportive family; Paul contracted non-paralytic polio as a child and his parents bought him skates during recovery, launching his lifelong involvement in the sport.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had skating domain expertise, though the family was supportive of his skating from a young age.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite skating club, sustained coaching, complementary partner, early specialization, polio recovery catalyst
evidence_summary: Paul recovered from childhood polio and began skating in Toronto, joining the Toronto Skating Club where Sheldon Galbraith (Barbara Ann Scott's coach) paired him with Barbara Wagner at age 15. They trained five hours a day, six days a week, plus intensive summer sessions, reaching World Championship gold by age 19. The partnership with Wagner was exceptionally durable and complementary, lasting eight years through Olympic gold. Galbraith's sustained, individualized coaching using film analysis and mirrors was a key accelerator.
starting_point: Born in Toronto to a supportive middle-class family; contracted non-paralytic polio as a child and his parents bought him skates during recovery.
current_position: Died on December 19, 2024 in Minneapolis, Minnesota at age 87; final career role was choreographer and director of choreography for Disney on Ice (1970-1986).

trajectory.event: Paired with Barbara Wagner by coach Sheldon Galbraith at the Toronto Skating Club.
Won first World Championship gold medal in pairs with Wagner, beginning a four-year reign.
Won Olympic gold medal in pairs at Squaw Valley and fourth consecutive World title; retired from amateur competition.
Joined Ice Capades as a professional skater, touring through 1964.
Began coaching in California; first student was Peggy Fleming, whom he coached to third at World Championships.
Began 16-year tenure as director of choreography for Walt Disney Corporation's skating productions.
Inducted into the World Figure Skating Hall of Fame.
Died peacefully on December 19, 2024 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

name: George Miller
milestone_by_age_26: Made a 60-second short film in 1971 (age 26) that won a student competition, but his breakthrough feature Mad Max did not arrive until 1979 (age 34); no material career milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Miller grew up in rural Queensland, Australia, the son of Greek immigrant parents who ran a cafe. He studied medicine at the University of New South Wales and developed an interest in filmmaking during his final year, making a one-minute short film in 1971 that earned entry to a film workshop where he met producing partner Byron Kennedy.
family_context_summary: Born to Greek immigrant parents Jim and Angela Miller in Chinchilla, Queensland, who ran a cafe in the small rural town.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had film or arts domain expertise.
evidence_summary: Miller's filmmaking career began with a student short film in 1971 during his final year of medical school, but his first feature film (Mad Max) was not released until 1979 when he was 34. No material, independently verifiable career milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Alexander Gustafsson
milestone_by_age_26: Fought Jon Jones for the UFC Light Heavyweight Championship at UFC 165 on September 21, 2013, at age 26, in a bout widely regarded as one of the greatest title fights in UFC history.
early_history_summary: Gustafsson grew up in the small town of Arboga, Sweden, and started boxing around age 10, winning the national youth championship at 16. After run-ins with the law including a prison sentence at 18 for assault, he discovered MMA in 2006 at age 19, turned professional in 2007, and signed with the UFC in 2009. He won his UFC debut at age 22 and compiled a 15-2 record to earn a title shot by 2013.
family_context_summary: Raised in Arboga, a small town in Sweden, by his father (a farmer) and step-mother; troubled youth with group affiliations and street fights led to a prison sentence at age 18.
primary_early_advantage_tags: boxing background, troubled youth catalyst, MMA wave, physical talent, UFC pipeline
evidence_summary: Gustafsson grew up in a small Swedish town with a troubled youth that included a prison sentence at 18; he used MMA as a turning point. His boxing background from age 10 provided a striking foundation, and the rising MMA wave in Europe gave him a platform. He joined Allstars Training Center in Stockholm and the UFC signed him at 22, leading to a title fight against Jon Jones at 26. His physical attributes (6'5", 79-inch reach) and natural fighting ability were key assets.
starting_point: Raised in Arboga, a small rural town in Sweden, by his father (a farmer) and step-mother; troubled youth with street fights and a prison sentence at age 18.
current_position: Retired from active UFC competition; last fought in July 2022 (loss to Nikita Krylov); inducted into UFC Hall of Fame Fight Wing in 2020 for first Jones fight; resides in Stockholm, Sweden.

trajectory.event: Won the Swedish national youth boxing championship.
Made professional MMA debut and won his first nine fights.
Signed with the UFC and won his debut at UFC 105 in November.

Inducted into the UFC Hall of Fame Fight Wing for the first Jon Jones fight.
Returned to light heavyweight but lost to Nikita Krylov at UFC Fight Night in London.

name: Domingo Perurena
milestone_by_age_26: Won Stage 18 of the 1966 Vuelta a España at age 22, the first of 12 career Vuelta stage wins, establishing himself as a top professional sprinter and climber.
early_history_summary: Perurena grew up in Oiartzun in the Basque Country of Spain, where he began cycling around age 14 with friends. He did not own his own bike until joining a juvenile team. As an amateur he won the Vuelta a Bidasoa (1964) and Tour d'Anjou (1965), then turned professional in 1965 with Mobylette GAC, winning Vuelta a Cantabria and a World Championship team time trial silver that year.
family_context_summary: Born in Oiartzun, Guipúzcoa, in the Basque Country of Spain; as a youth he helped run a bar with friends and did not own a bicycle until joining a juvenile cycling team.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had cycling domain expertise, though the Basque Country has a deep cycling culture.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Basque cycling culture, early pro transition, team pipeline, climbing and sprinting ability
evidence_summary: Perurena emerged from the Basque Country, one of cycling's deepest talent regions, and began riding around age 14 with friends before joining a juvenile team. He progressed through amateur teams (Nuarbe, Olarra) and turned professional at 21 in 1965, immediately winning Vuelta a Cantabria and a World Championship team time trial silver. His Basque geography provided immersion in cycling culture and access to professional team structures (Fagor, Kas-Kaskol) that accelerated his career.
starting_point: Born in Oiartzun, Basque Country, Spain; from a modest background, did not own a bicycle until joining a juvenile cycling team around age 14.
current_position: Died on June 8, 2023 in San Sebastián at age 79; had been a team manager for multiple Spanish cycling teams (Teka, Orbea, Euskadi) after retiring from riding.

trajectory.event: Turned professional with Mobylette GAC; won Vuelta a Cantabria and World Championship team time trial silver.

Won the Tour de France mountains classification and a second Vuelta points classification.
Finished second overall at the Vuelta a España and won the Spanish National Road Race Championships again.
Died on June 8, 2023 in San Sebastián, Spain.

name: Oh Eun-sun
milestone_by_age_26: No material mountaineering milestone by age 26; she was a civil servant and amateur climber during this period, with her first 8000m summit (Gasherbrum II) not occurring until 1997 at age 31.
early_history_summary: Oh was born in Namwon, South Korea, and her family moved to Seoul where she took up rock climbing in high school. She studied computer science at the University of Suwon and joined the mountaineering club. After graduation she worked as a civil servant in Seoul before leaving the job in the early 1990s to pursue mountaineering full-time.
family_context_summary: Born in Namwon, North Jeolla Province; father was in the South Korean military and the family moved often before settling in Seoul.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had mountaineering domain expertise.
evidence_summary: Oh was an amateur climber and civil servant through her mid-twenties. Her first major mountaineering achievement was reaching 7,300m on Everest in 1993 at age 27 (without summiting), and her first 8000m summit was Gasherbrum II in 1997 at age 31. No material mountaineering milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Lars Vilks
milestone_by_age_26: No material artistic milestone by age 26; he was painting in the 1970s but his first major work (Nimis) was not created until 1980 at age 34, and his doctoral degree came in 1987.
early_history_summary: Vilks was born in Helsingborg, Sweden, to a father of Estonian and Latvian descent and a Swedish mother. He started painting in the 1970s as a self-taught artist while pursuing academic studies in art history at Lund University. His first significant artwork, the driftwood sculpture Nimis, was not begun until 1980 when he was 34.
family_context_summary: Born in Helsingborg, Sweden; father was of Estonian and Latvian descent, mother was Swedish.

name: Peter Post
milestone_by_age_26: Won Six-Day track races in 1959 at age 25, establishing himself as a dominant force in professional six-day racing; he would go on to win 65 Six-Day races in his career.
early_history_summary: Post was born in Amsterdam as the eighth child of a butcher's family and grew up during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. He began cycling making deliveries for his father's shop and won the Amsterdam Championship for Butcher Boys in 1949. A neighbor spotted his talent and introduced him to cycling; he obtained his first racing license in 1952 and turned professional in 1956 with RIH Sport, riding alongside track specialist Gerrit Schulte.
family_context_summary: Born in Amsterdam as the eighth of thirteen children in a butcher's family; grew up in poverty during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, making deliveries on a heavy transport bike for his father's shop.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented that parents had cycling expertise; however, neighbor Piet Schulte (brother of cyclist Gerrit Schulte) spotted his talent and introduced him to the sport.
primary_early_advantage_tags: delivery cycling, Amsterdam cycling culture, neighbor mentor, Nazi occupation hardship, track racing specialization
evidence_summary: Post grew up in a large butcher's family in Amsterdam during WWII, delivering goods on a heavy bike which built his cycling foundation. A neighbor (brother of pro cyclist Gerrit Schulte) spotted his talent and nudged him into racing, against his father's wishes. He secretly assembled a racing bike and joined a youth cycling club, turning professional in 1956. His immersion in Amsterdam's cycling culture and direct domain exposure from delivery riding provided a strong base for his track racing dominance.
starting_point: Born in Amsterdam as the eighth of thirteen children in a butcher's family; grew up in poverty during the Nazi occupation, making deliveries on a heavy transport bike for his father's shop.
current_position: Died on January 14, 2011 in Amstelveen at age 77; final career role was directeur sportif, most notably founding and managing TI-Raleigh (1974-1983) and Panasonic-Raleigh (1984-1992), revolutionizing professional cycling team management.

trajectory.event: Won the Amsterdam Championship for Butcher Boys on a delivery bike.
Obtained his first racing license after secretly joining a youth cycling club.
Turned professional with RIH Sport, riding alongside track specialist Gerrit Schulte.
Won his first Six-Day track races, establishing dominance in professional six-day racing.
Won the Ronde van Nederland overall classification.
Became Dutch national road race champion and won the Tour of Belgium.
Won Paris-Roubaix at the fastest-ever average speed for a major Classic (45.131 km/h).
Died on January 14, 2011 in Amstelveen, Netherlands.

name: Christian Boltanski
milestone_by_age_26: Had his first solo exhibition, 'La vie impossible de Christian Boltanski,' at the Théâtre Le Ranelagh in Paris in May 1968, at age 23, marking his entry into the professional art world.
early_history_summary: Boltanski was born in Paris ten days after the liberation, to a Jewish physician father who had hidden under floorboards during the occupation and a Corsican Catholic mother who was a writer. He dropped out of school at 12 and began painting at 13, living in considerable isolation and producing hundreds of paintings and expressionist dolls through his early twenties before his first solo show in 1968.
family_context_summary: Born in Paris to a Jewish physician father of Russian origin who hid under floorboards during WWII, and a Corsican Catholic mother who was a novelist; grew up in a bohemian, intellectually rich but trauma-marked household.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a physician and mother was a writer (pen name Annie Lauran), providing an intellectual and culturally sophisticated household, though not specifically in the visual arts.
primary_early_advantage_tags: WWII trauma, self-taught artist, Paris art scene, intellectual family, isolation-driven creation
evidence_summary: Boltanski's childhood was profoundly shaped by his father's wartime hiding and the family's constant fear, which fueled his obsessive early art production. He dropped out of school at 12 and painted hundreds of works in isolation through his early twenties, supported by parents who accepted his unconventional path. His mother's friend opened a gallery where he met other artists, providing entry to the Paris art world. The combination of trauma, intellectual family background, and Paris's cultural ecosystem enabled his first solo exhibition at 23.
starting_point: Born in Paris to a Jewish physician father (who hid under floorboards during WWII) and a Corsican Catholic mother who was a novelist; grew up in a bohemian, trauma-marked intellectual household.
current_position: Died on July 14, 2021 in Paris at age 76; was one of France's most internationally renowned contemporary artists, known for large-scale photography and installation works exhibited at major museums worldwide.

trajectory.event: Began painting after dropping out of school at age 12, producing large-format figurative works with macabre themes.
Had first solo exhibition 'La vie impossible de Christian Boltanski' at the Théâtre Le Ranelagh in Paris.
Produced first artist's book 'Recherche et présentation de tout ce qui reste de mon enfance 1944-1950' at Givaudan gallery.
Began creating large-scale mixed-media installations that would define his mature practice.
Represented France at the Venice Biennale, cementing his international reputation.
Major retrospective 'No Man's Land' presented at the Grand Palais in Paris.
Died on July 14, 2021 in Paris; honored with tributes at Versailles, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre.

name: Rimas Kurtinaitis
milestone_by_age_26: Won the USSR national basketball championship in 1982 at age 22, the first of four USSR titles, playing for CSKA Moscow and later Žalgiris Kaunas in one of the world's strongest basketball leagues.
early_history_summary: Kurtinaitis grew up in Kaunas, Lithuania (then Soviet Union), a city with a deep basketball culture. He began basketball training in the third grade at the Kaunas basketball school under coach Edvardas Nekrašas. He progressed through Soviet club teams, playing for Panevėžys Lietkabelis (1979-80), Riga ASK (1980-81), and CSKA Moscow (1981-82) before joining Žalgiris Kaunas in 1982, where he won multiple USSR championships and became a Soviet national team member.
family_context_summary: Born in Kaunas, Lithuanian SSR, to a modest working-class family; siblings shared limited resources such as a single winter jacket, typical of working-class Soviet Lithuanian households.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had basketball domain expertise, though Kaunas was a basketball-crazy city with strong youth programs.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kaunas basketball school, Soviet club pipeline, early specialization, Žalgiris system, modest background catalyst
evidence_summary: Kurtinaitis benefited from Kaunas's deep basketball culture and the Soviet sports pipeline, starting structured training in the third grade at the Kaunas basketball school. The Soviet system's elite club structure (CSKA Moscow, Žalgiris Kaunas) provided a high-performance pipeline that accelerated his development. His modest background in Soviet Lithuania created urgency and motivation. By 22, he was a USSR champion, and by 25, a European champion with the Soviet national team.
starting_point: Born in Kaunas, Lithuanian SSR, to a modest working-class family in Soviet-era Lithuania; siblings shared limited resources such as a single winter jacket.
current_position: Serves as head coach of the Lithuania men's national basketball team; previously coached CSKA Moscow and Khimki to multiple EuroLeague and VTB United League titles; resides in Lithuania.

trajectory.event: Began basketball training at the Kaunas basketball school under coach Edvardas Nekrašas.
Won the USSR national basketball championship, the first of four USSR titles.

Won the FIBA Intercontinental Cup (William Jones Cup) with Žalgiris Kaunas and was world vice-champion with the USSR.
Won Olympic gold medal with the Soviet Union at the Seoul Olympics.
Won Olympic bronze medal with the newly independent Lithuania at the Barcelona Olympics.
Won European championship silver medal with Lithuania in Athens.
Won second Olympic bronze medal with Lithuania at the Atlanta Olympics.

name: Valentina Stenina
milestone_by_age_26: Won the World Allround Speed Skating Championship in 1960 at age 25, becoming world champion and Olympic silver medalist in the same year.
early_history_summary: Stenina was born in Babruysk, Belarus, and fled with her mother to Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg) in 1941 during WWII. She took up speed skating in Sverdlovsk, training at VSS Trud, where she met and married fellow skater Boris Stenin. She placed fourth at her first Soviet Championships in 1957, won her first medals in 1958, and won World Championship silver in 1959 before becoming World Allround champion in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in Babruysk, Belarus; fled with her mother to Sverdlovsk during WWII as a refugee, where she took up speed skating at VSS Trud sports society.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had skating expertise; mother was a war refugee who relocated her during WWII.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, VSS Trud, husband-skater partnership, WWII displacement, Sverdlovsk skating hub
evidence_summary: Stenina's career was shaped by the Soviet sports pipeline: as a WWII refugee in Sverdlovsk, she entered the VSS Trud sports society and was immersed in the Soviet speed skating development system. Her marriage to fellow skater Boris Stenin created a uniquely complementary partnership where both became World Allround champions in the same year (1960). The Soviet system's institutional support, combined with her husband's mutual training partnership, accelerated her rise from first Soviet Championships appearance in 1957 to World champion by 1960.
starting_point: Born in Babruysk, Belarus; fled with her mother to Sverdlovsk as a WWII refugee in 1941, where she took up speed skating at the VSS Trud sports society.
current_position: Living in Yekaterinburg (formerly Sverdlovsk), Russia, at age 91; retired from competitive speed skating in 1968 after a career as a three-time World Allround champion and two-time Olympic silver medalist.

trajectory.event: Competed at her first Soviet Championships, placing fourth in the 5,000m.
Won silver medal at the World Allround Speed Skating Championships in Sverdlovsk.
Won World Allround Championship gold and Olympic silver in the 3,000m at Squaw Valley.
Won her second World Allround Championship title and first Soviet all-around national title.
Won second Olympic silver medal in the 3,000m at Innsbruck.
Won her third World Allround Championship title.
Awarded Honorable Citizen of Sverdlovsk; won fourth Soviet national all-around title.
Retired from competitive speed skating and moved to Moscow to coach with husband Boris.

name: Ryszard Kukliński
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; he was a junior military officer who had graduated from the Officers' Infantry Academy in 1950, with his notable achievements (CIA espionage, colonel rank) coming after age 34.
early_history_summary: Kukliński was born in Warsaw to a working-class family with Catholic and socialist traditions. His father joined the Polish resistance during WWII and died in Sachsenhausen concentration camp in 1943. After the war, Kukliński joined the Polish Workers' Party in 1946 and entered the Officers' Infantry Academy in Wrocław in 1947, graduating as a warrant officer in 1950 at age 20.
family_context_summary: Born in Warsaw to a working-class family with strong Catholic and socialist traditions; father was in the Polish resistance and died in Sachsenhausen concentration camp in 1943.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had military or intelligence domain expertise, though father's resistance activity exposed Kukliński to themes of patriotic duty.
evidence_summary: Kukliński graduated from the Officers' Infantry Academy at age 20 and was a junior officer in the Polish People's Army through his twenties. His significant career milestones — work in espionage and counterintelligence (1964, age 34), CIA cooperation (1972, age 42), and colonel rank — all occurred well after age 26. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26.

name: Antonio Roldán
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Olympic gold medal in boxing (featherweight) at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics at age 22, the first Mexican to win boxing gold at a home Olympics.
early_history_summary: Roldán grew up in the San Simón neighborhood of Mexico City and originally dreamed of becoming a professional footballer. At age 15, he lied to a boxing promoter about having 14 amateur fights to get his first bout, which he won by decision. He developed as an amateur boxer and earned a spot on the Mexican Olympic team for the 1968 Mexico City Games, where he won gold in the featherweight division.
family_context_summary: Born in Mexico City; grew up in the San Simón neighborhood in a working-class environment where he played street football and fought with neighborhood kids.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources that parents had boxing domain expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: working-class neighborhood, self-initiated boxing entry, home Olympics advantage, physical talent, street fighting background
evidence_summary: Roldán came from a working-class Mexico City neighborhood where street fighting was common, and he entered boxing through self-initiative by lying to a promoter to get his first fight at 15. The 1968 Mexico City Olympics provided a unique home-soil advantage that amplified his talent. His physical ability and determination carried him from a complete novice to Olympic gold in just seven years, though his subsequent professional career was undistinguished (5-3 record).
starting_point: Born in Mexico City to a working-class family in the San Simón neighborhood; grew up playing street football and fighting with neighborhood kids.
current_position: Living in Mexico City at age 80; runs a sporting goods business with his family; retired from boxing in 1974 after a brief professional career (5 wins, 3 losses).
